title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: He didn't leave for Cambridge the next day as he'd said he would. He delayed his departure a full week. During that time he made me feel what severe punishment a good yet stern, conscientious yet unforgiving man can inflict on someone who has offended him. Without a single hostile act, without one reproachful word, he managed to impress on me constantly that I had been cast out of his favor.

Not that St. John harbored any spirit of unchristian revenge—not that he would have harmed a hair on my head if he could. By both nature and principle, he was above petty vengeance. He had forgiven me for saying I scorned him and his love. But he had not forgotten the words. As long as he and I both lived, he never would forget them. I saw by his look, whenever he turned to me, that they hung permanently in the air between us. Whenever I spoke, they sounded in my voice. They colored my every word and action.

He didn't stop talking to me. He even called me each morning to join him at his desk as usual. But I fear the imperfect human inside him took a pleasure the pure Christian did not share—pleasure in showing how skillfully he could, while acting and speaking exactly as always, drain every drop of warmth and interest from his words and manner. To me, he had become nothing more than a marble guardian angel. He was still protecting me, still watching over me, but the kindness had turned to ice.

All this was torture—refined, lingering torture. It kept up a slow fire of frustration and a trembling grief that wore me down completely. I felt how—if I were his wife—this good man, pure as a deep, sunless spring, could slowly kill me without drawing a single drop of blood, and without staining his crystal conscience with even the faintest mark of crime. I felt this especially when I tried to make peace. No compassion met mine. He felt no suffering in return. He hadn't given himself to me or tried to win me. He stood apart from me as if we were different species. He was quietly confident that he was right, and I was wrong. This conviction showed clearly in everything he said and did.

The night before he was to leave, I happened to see him walking in the garden at sunset. Remembering that this man, distant as he now was, had once saved my life—and that we were family—I was moved to make one last attempt at friendship. I went out and approached him at the little gate. I spoke directly.
"St. John, I'm unhappy because you're still angry with me. Let us be friends."
"I hope we are friends," came the unmoved reply. He continued watching the rising moon.
"No, St. John, we are not friends as we were. You know that."
"Aren't we? That's wrong. For my part, I wish you no ill and all good."
"I believe you, St. John. I'm sure you're incapable of wishing anyone ill. But as your relative, I want something more than the general goodwill you extend to strangers."
"Of course," he said. "Your wish is reasonable. And I'm far from considering you a stranger."

This, spoken in a cool, even tone, was both humiliating and baffling. If I'd listened to my pride, I would have walked away at once. But something worked in me more powerfully than pride. I deeply respected my cousin's talent and principles. His friendship meant a great deal to me. Losing it was hard to bear. I wouldn't give up the attempt to regain it so easily.
"Must we part this way, St. John? When you go to India, will you leave me like this—without a kinder word than any you've yet spoken?"
He turned from the moon and faced me.
"When I go to India, Jane, will I leave you? What! Are you not going to India?"
"You said I couldn't unless I married you."
"And you will not marry me? You hold to that decision?"

Reader, do you know, as I do, the terror that cold people can put into the ice of their questions? How much of an avalanche is in their anger? How much of a frozen sea breaking apart is in their displeasure?
"No. St. John, I will not marry you. I stand by my decision."
The avalanche had shaken and shifted slightly forward. But it hadn't crashed down yet.
"Once more, why this refusal?" he asked.
"Before," I answered, "because you didn't love me. Now, because you almost hate me. If I married you, you would kill me. You are killing me now."
His lips and cheeks turned white—deathly white.

"I should kill you—I am killing you? Those words should not be used. They are violent, unfeminine, and untrue. They reveal an unfortunate state of mind. They deserve severe correction. They would seem inexcusable, except that it is man's duty to forgive his fellow even seventy-seven times over."
I had done it now. In trying to erase the mark of my earlier offense from his mind, I had stamped a new one—far deeper. I had burned it in.
"Now you will truly hate me," I said. "It's useless to try to make peace. I've made an eternal enemy of you."
These words inflicted a fresh wound—worse because they touched on the truth. That bloodless lip trembled briefly. I knew the steel-hard anger I had sharpened. My heart ached.
"You completely misread my words," I said, seizing his hand. "I had no intention of hurting you—truly, I didn't."
He smiled bitterly and pulled his hand firmly away. "And now I suppose you're taking back your promise to go to India altogether?" he said after a long pause.
"Yes, I'll still go—as your assistant," I answered.

A very long silence followed. What struggle between nature and duty took place in him during that pause, I cannot say. Only strange gleams flickered in his eyes, and dark shadows crossed his face. At last he spoke.

"I've already explained why a single woman of your age cannot accompany a single man of mine abroad. I explained it in terms that, I would have thought, would prevent you from ever mentioning the plan again. That you've done so, I regret—for your sake."

I cut in. Any clear reproach actually gave me courage. "Stick to common sense, St. John—you're drifting into nonsense. You pretend to be shocked by what I've said. You're not really shocked. With your intelligence, you can't be so dense or so vain as to misunderstand me. I say again: I will be your assistant, if you like, but never your wife."
Again he turned deathly pale. But, as before, he controlled his emotions perfectly. He answered firmly but calmly—

"A female assistant who is not my wife would never work. So it seems you cannot go with me. But if you're sincere in your offer, I will, while in town, speak to a married missionary whose wife needs help. Your own fortune will make you independent of the Society's aid. And so you may still be spared the dishonor of breaking your promise and abandoning the group you agreed to join."
Now, I had never, as the reader knows, made any formal promise or entered into any commitment. This language was far too harsh and far too dictatorial for the situation. I replied—

"There is no dishonor, no broken promise, no abandonment here. I am under no obligation whatsoever to go to India—especially with strangers. With you I would have risked a great deal, because I admire you, trust you, and love you as a sister. But I'm convinced that wherever I went, and with whomever, I would not survive long in that climate."
"Ah! You're afraid of yourself," he said, curling his lip.

"I am. God did not give me my life to throw away. To do as you wish would be nearly the same as suicide. And besides, before I make any final decision about leaving England, I need to know for certain whether I can't do more good by staying than by going."
"What do you mean?"
"It would be pointless to explain. But there's a question that has tormented me for a long time. I can't go anywhere until it's resolved."

"I know where your heart turns and what it clings to. The attachment you cherish is sinful and unsanctioned. You should have destroyed it long ago. Now you should be ashamed even to mention it. You're thinking of Mr. Rochester."
It was true. My silence confessed it.
"Are you going to look for Mr. Rochester?"
"I must find out what has become of him."

"Then it remains for me," he said, "to remember you in my prayers and to earnestly ask God that you may not become lost. I had thought I recognized in you one of the chosen. But God sees differently from man. His will be done—"
He opened the gate, passed through, and walked away down the glen. He was soon out of sight.
Back in the parlour, I found Diana standing at the window, looking thoughtful. Diana was much taller than me. She put her hand on my shoulder and, bending down, studied my face.

"Jane," she said, "you're always pale and upset now. I'm sure something is wrong. Tell me what's going on between you and St. John. I've been watching you from the window for half an hour. Forgive me for spying, but for a long time I've had a feeling—I hardly know what. St. John is a strange person—"
She paused. I didn't speak. Soon she continued—
"My brother has special views of some kind about you, I'm sure. He has singled you out with an attention and interest he's never shown anyone else. To what end? I wish he loved you—does he, Jane?"
I pressed her cool hand to my hot forehead. "No, Diana. Not one bit."
"Then why does he follow you with his eyes, and get you alone with him so often, and keep you constantly at his side? Mary and I both decided he wanted to marry you."
"He does—he has asked me to be his wife."
Diana clapped her hands. "That's exactly what we hoped and expected! And you'll marry him, Jane, won't you? And then he'll stay in England."
"Far from it, Diana. His only reason for proposing is to find a suitable partner for his work in India."
"What! He wants you to go to India?"
"Yes."
"Madness!" she exclaimed. "You wouldn't survive three months there—I'm certain. You must never go. You haven't agreed, have you, Jane?"
"I've refused to marry him—"
"And that upset him?" she suggested.
"Deeply. He'll never forgive me, I'm afraid. But I offered to go with him as his sister."

"That was reckless, Jane. Think of the task you'd be taking on—constant exhaustion, the kind that kills even the strong. And you're not strong. St. John—you know him—would push you to impossible limits. He'd allow no rest during the worst heat. And unfortunately, I've noticed, whatever he demands, you force yourself to do. I'm amazed you found the courage to refuse his hand. You don't love him then, Jane?"
"Not as a husband."
"Yet he's a handsome man."
"And I'm so plain, Diana. We'd never suit."
"Plain? You? Not at all. You're much too pretty, as well as too good, to be roasted alive in Calcutta." And again she urged me to give up all thoughts of going with her brother.

"I must," I said. "Just now, when I repeated my offer to serve as his assistant, he was appalled by my lack of propriety. He seemed to think I'd done something indecent in proposing to travel with him unmarried—as if I hadn't always hoped to find a brother in him and regarded him as one."
"What makes you say he doesn't love you, Jane?"

"You should hear him on the subject. He has explained again and again that it's not himself but his mission he wants to pair with a wife. He has told me I'm made for work, not for love—which is true, no doubt. But in my view, if I'm not made for love, it follows that I'm not made for marriage. Wouldn't it be strange, Diana, to be chained for life to a man who saw you only as a useful tool?"
"Unbearable—unnatural—absolutely out of the question!"

"And then," I continued, "though I feel only sisterly affection for him now, if forced to be his wife, I can imagine developing an unavoidable, strange, agonizing kind of love for him. Because he is so talented, and there's often a certain heroic grandeur in his look and manner. In that case, my life would become unspeakably wretched. He wouldn't want me to love him. And if I showed my feelings, he'd make me understand they were unwanted and excessive. Superfluous. I know he would."
"And yet St. John is a good man," said Diana.

"He is a good and great man. But he forgets, mercilessly, the feelings and needs of ordinary people when pursuing his own grand vision. It's better, therefore, for the small to stay out of his way—or be trampled underfoot. Here he comes! I'll leave you, Diana." And I hurried upstairs as I saw him entering the garden.

But I was forced to face him again at supper. During the meal he appeared just as composed as usual. I had thought he would barely speak to me, and I was certain he had abandoned his marriage plan. The rest of the evening proved me wrong on both counts. He addressed me exactly in his usual manner—or what had lately become his usual manner—carefully polite. No doubt he had called on the Holy Spirit to subdue the anger I'd provoked, and now believed he had forgiven me. But I saw he had not. It was there in every measured word and controlled gesture. The forgiveness was a performance. Beneath it, the steel remained.

For the evening reading before prayers, he chose the twenty-first chapter of Revelation. It was always a pleasure to listen to his voice read the Bible. Never did it sound so sweet and full—never was his manner so impressive in its noble simplicity—as when he delivered the words of God. Tonight that voice took a more solemn tone and his manner a more thrilling quality. He sat amid his household circle—the May moon shining softly through the window—and read of the new heaven and new earth. Of the river of the water of life, and the tree with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding fruit every month. Of the city with no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God was its light.
The words that followed thrilled me strangely—especially as I felt, by a slight, indescribable shift in his voice, that in speaking them his eyes had turned to me.

"He that overcomes shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. But"—he read slowly, distinctly—"the fearful, the unbelieving, and so forth, shall have their part in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death."
From that moment, I knew what fate St. John feared for me.

A calm, subdued triumph—blended with yearning earnestness—marked his reading of the last glorious verses of that chapter. He believed his own name was already written in the Lamb's book of life. He longed for the hour that would admit him to the city to which the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor. The city that needs no sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God lights it, and the Lamb is its lamp.

In the prayer that followed, all his energy gathered and all his stern passion awoke. He was in deep earnest, wrestling with God, determined to prevail. He begged for strength for the fainthearted. He asked for guidance for wanderers from the fold—for a return, even at the last moment, for those being lured from the narrow path. He pleaded for a brand snatched from the burning. Earnestness is always deeply solemn. First, as I listened, I was moved. Then, as the prayer went on, I felt troubled. Was this prayer for me? Was I the one being prayed for? A shiver ran through me.

The prayer over, we said our goodbyes. He was leaving very early in the morning. Diana and Mary kissed him and left the room—prompted, I think, by a whispered hint from him. I offered my hand and wished him a pleasant journey.

"Thank you, Jane. As I said, I'll return from Cambridge in two weeks. That time is yours for reflection. If I listened to human pride, I would say nothing more about marriage. But I listen to my duty, and I keep my first aim firmly in view—to do all things for the glory of God. My Master was patient, and so will I be. I cannot abandon you to ruin. Repent—decide, while there's still time. Remember, we're told to work while it is day—warned that the night comes when no one can work. Remember the fate of Dives, who had his good things in this life. God give you strength to choose the better part which shall not be taken from you!"

He laid his hand on my head as he spoke these last words. He had spoken earnestly, gently. His look was not that of a lover gazing at his beloved, but that of a pastor calling back his wandering sheep—or better, a guardian angel watching over the soul in his care. All men of talent, whether they feel deeply or not—whether they are zealots or despots—if only they are sincere—have their moments of mastery, when they command and rule. I felt reverence for St. John. I felt his power. But the power was not mine to submit to. I would follow him to the ends of the earth. I would not give him my hand.

I stood motionless under my guide's touch. My refusals were forgotten—my fears overcome—my resistance paralyzed. The impossible—my marriage to St. John—was rapidly becoming possible. Everything was shifting with a sudden sweep. Religion called—angels beckoned—God commanded—life rolled together like a scroll—death's gates opening, showed eternity beyond. It seemed that for safety and bliss in the next world, everything in this one could be sacrificed in an instant. The dim room was full of visions.

"Could you decide now?" asked the missionary. The question was put gently. He drew me to him, also gently. Oh, that gentleness! How much more powerful it was than force! I could resist St. John's anger. But I grew soft as a reed under his kindness. Yet I knew—if I gave in now, I would still be made to regret my earlier resistance. His nature had not changed in one hour of solemn prayer. It was only lifted up.
"I could decide if I were only sure," I answered. "If I were only convinced that it is God's will that I marry you, I could vow to do it here and now—come what may afterward!"

"My prayers are heard!" St. John exclaimed. He pressed his hand more firmly on my head, as if claiming me. He put his arm around me—almost as if he loved me. I say almost—I knew the difference. I had felt what it was to be loved. But, like him, I had now pushed love aside and thought only of duty. I struggled against the dimness clouding my vision, behind which something still churned. Sincerely, deeply, urgently, I longed to do what was right—and only that. "Show me, show me the path!" I begged of Heaven.

The house was completely still. I believe everyone except St. John and me had gone to bed. The single candle was dying out. The room was full of moonlight. My heart beat fast and hard—I could hear its throb. Suddenly it stopped, seized by a feeling beyond description. The feeling was not like an electric shock, but it was just as sharp, strange, and startling. It acted on my senses as if they had been asleep until now, and were suddenly jolted wide awake. They rose, expectant—eye and ear waiting. The flesh trembled on my bones.
"What did you hear? What do you see?" asked St. John. I saw nothing, but I heard a voice somewhere cry—
"Jane! Jane! Jane!"—nothing more.
"Oh God! What is it?" I gasped.

I might have said, "Where is it?" For it didn't seem to come from the room—nor the house—nor the garden. It came not from the air, nor from under the earth, nor from above. I had heard it—but from where, it was impossible to know! And it was the voice of a human being—a known, loved, well-remembered voice—the voice of Edward Fairfax Rochester. And it spoke in pain and sorrow, wildly, eerily, urgently.
"I am coming!" I cried. "Wait for me! Oh, I will come!" I flew to the door and looked into the passage—it was dark. I ran out into the garden—it was empty.
"Where are you?" I called out.
The hills beyond Marsh Glen sent the answer faintly back—"Where are you?" I listened. The wind sighed low in the fir trees. All was moorland loneliness and midnight silence.

"Down, superstition!" I told myself, as that phantom rose up dark beside the black yew tree at the gate. "This is not deception, nor witchcraft. It is the work of nature. She was stirred, and she performed—no miracle—but her finest work."

I broke away from St. John, who had followed and would have held me back. It was my turn to take command. My powers were awake and active. I told him not to question or comment. I told him to leave me alone. I must and would be alone. He obeyed at once. Where there is energy to command well enough, obedience never fails. I went up to my room, locked myself in, fell on my knees, and prayed in my own way—a different way from St. John's, but effective in its own fashion. I seemed to reach beyond the visible world, as it were—very near a mighty Spirit. And my soul rushed out in gratitude. Not through words. Through something deeper. I rose from my knees. I knew what I had to do.
